title: Pacing lanes orchestration and granular burst policies (PRD sketch)
summary: Sketch for a tenant-facing orchestration model that introduces 'pacing lanes' — lightweight, rentable runtime lanes with configurable budgets and escalation policies. Goal is to provide predictable SLOs while enabling controlled short-term bursts and soft isolation across dedicated pools.
goals: 1) Give tenants clear, enforceable capacity lanes (stable/opportunistic/emergency) with documented latencies and costs. 2) Let operators safely offer short bursts while preserving core SLOs for high-tier customers. 3) Support autoscale decisions using lane-aware signals so scaling is smoother and cost-predictable.
background: Current dedicated offering supports reserved capacity and many ad-hoc burst behaviors. Engineering struggles with tenants oversubscribing shared burst pools, causing noisy neighbor effects. Existing proposals address eviction and credit pools but lack a tenant-visible, policy-driven construct that ties budget, latency, and escalation together. Pacing lanes are an attempt to unify these controls into a single orchestration primitive.
user_stories: As a platform admin, I want per-tenant lanes with budgets so I can limit short-term spike impact on other tenants.
As a customer, I want a predictable burst contract (e.g., 5 minutes at 3x baseline) with clear fallbacks if unavailable.
As an SRE, I want telemetry that shows lane-level latency percentiles so I can tune lane sizes and prewarm settings.
As a product manager, I want lane-based pricing so we can offer cheaper opportunistic lanes and premium stable lanes with SLAs.
proposal:
Introduce three canonical lanes per tenant by default: stable, opportunistic, and emergency. Stable is backed by reserved capacity and has tight latency SLOs. Opportunistic is served from shared burst pools with best-effort latency and a credits budget. Emergency is a small fast-fail lane for critical requests routed to higher-cost fallbacks (e.g., smaller models, faster instances) when stable is exhausted. Each lane has:
- Budget window (tokens/minute and bucket size)
- Latency SLA target (p50/p95)
- Escalation policy (soft-degrade -> fallback model -> reject)
- Chargeback cost multiplier
Autoscaling decisions are lane-aware: stable lane expansion requires reserve commit or tenant approval; opportunistic autoscale uses opportunistic pool headroom with rate-limited borrow; emergency uses hot-path fallbacks without scaling underlying pool.
architecture_overview:
Key components:
- Lane Manager (control plane): stores lane configs, budgets, and escalation policies.
- Token Gate (runtime): continuous token accounting, enforces per-request lane admission.
- Lane Broker (routing): maps incoming requests to available lanes, applies fallback ordering.
- Credit Ledger: tenant-level ledger for opportunistic credits and earn/spend hooks.
- Observability: lane-level dashboards, cost breakout, and alerting hooks.
Runtime integration: Token Gate sits in front of the request router. If a stable lane token is available, request proceeds to dedicated replica. If not and opportunistic tokens exist, route to opportunistic pool. If all fail and emergency policy allows, apply emergency fallback chain.
Note: lane configs should be declarative and editable via the Console and API.
policy_examples: Tenant A (gold): stable: 200 tok/min, p95 < 120ms; opportunistic: 500 tok/min bucket (replenish 100/min); emergency: 20 tok/min -> fallback to smaller-llama-7b-fast model
Tenant B (startup): stable: 50 tok/min, opportunistic: 200 tok/min bucket (replenish 40/min), emergency disabled
Operator policy: if opportunistic pool saturation > 80% for 5m, temporarily reduce opportunistic replenishment by 30% across low-tier tenants
api_examples:
PATCH /v1/tenants/{id}/lanes 
{ lane_config: { stable: {reservations: 8, tokens_per_min: 200}, opportunistic: {bucket: 500, replenish_per_min: 100}, emergency: {tokens_per_min:20, fallbacks:["tiny-v1"]} } }
ops_considerations:
- Fairness: need an enforcement window to prevent burst cycling abuse.
- Prewarming: stable lane should support explicit prewarm and warm-start hints for models with long startup.
- Accounting latency: token accounting must be strongly consistent for correctness but we can allow eventual reconciliation for opportunistic lane charges.
- Safety: Automatic global throttles if opportunistic pools exceed safe thresholds.
- Backfills: Define behavior when a tenant's committed reserve shrinks (grace window + credit refund policy).
metrics_and_slos: Burst acceptance rate (requests allowed vs rejected)
Number of escalations to fallback per tenant per week
rollout_plan: Phase 1 (internal beta): implement Lane Manager + Token Gate in staging; enable for 5 internal tenants and observe. Phase 2 (select customers): expose lane configs in Console for opt-in customers, add billing prototype. Phase 3 (general availability): open lanes to all dedicated tenants, documented SLAs, and pricing. Each phase includes a canary safety threshold and rollback plan. Expected timeline: 3 months to Phase 1, 3 months to Phase 2, 2 months to GA after signoffs.
operational_playbook: If opportunistic pool saturated -> reduce replenishment, notify growth and sales. If stable lane p95SLO breaches persist -> auto-open RCA ticket, consider temporary reserve bump or migrate noisy tenant to isolated pool. For token ledger divergence -> pause opportunistic credit consumption and run reconciliation job. Major incidents require lane-level timeline in postmortem.
open_questions: How granular should default lanes be? (3 canonical vs. customizable N lanes)
What billing model for opportunistic credits — subscription vs pay-as-you-burn?
How to handle cross-tenant borrow during global events (large model release spikes)?
What is the correct reconciliation window for opportunistic token accounting to avoid billing disputes?
appendix: Related ideas we chose not to pursue in this PRD: hard per-tenant physical isolation by default (too costly), opaque best-effort pools with no tenant visibility (makes cost/latency unpredictable), guaranteed burst leases >1h (operationally risky). References: earlier dedicated capacity drafts in this folder and SLO playbooks.
